commands.name: caveman
commands.description: Terse caveman voice: answer first, fluff gone, every technical fact kept. Use for /caveman, "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "be brief", "less tokens". Stays on until "stop caveman" or "normal mode". (user)

commands.name: handoff
commands.description: Write a handoff document another agent can resume this work from — what the task is, what is done, what is left, and how to verify it. Use on a HARNESS CHECKPOINT, or when asked to hand off, checkpoint or pause work for another agent or host. (user)

commands.name: harness
commands.description: Operate the Harness agent fleet for this project — `/harness <idea>` takes an idea to a running fleet in one conversation (install, init, grill into a PRD, start); first-time SETUP (init, seed labels, start) and day-to-day operate (pause/resume/update/status, watch sessions, unstick the GitHub-issue board). Trigger on /harness or requests like "set up the fleet", "start the fleet", "pause the agents", "what's the harness doing". (user)

commands.name: harness-arc
commands.description: Deploy a large multi-plan design to a Harness fleet as a sequenced chain of PRDs that runs unattended to completion, with a wayfinder map holding the decisions the fleet cannot make; `harness supervise` catches the fleet's silent stall modes. Use when a spec or design is too big for one PRD, when the user wants a fleet to run "fully automatic until shipped", when deploying an implementation plan of several plans/stages, or when asked to watch, babysit, or unstick a running Harness fleet. (user)

commands.name: harness-init
commands.description: First-time Harness setup — run the wizard that writes .harness/config and seeds GitHub labels. Trigger on /harness-init or "set up the harness config". (user)

commands.name: harness-issue
commands.description: Inject a discrete implementation issue (or a few) into a LIVE Harness fleet — grill the requirement, confirm a crystallized brief, then launch the headless injector. Trigger on /harness-issue or "add a task to the running fleet". (user)

commands.name: harness-one
commands.description: Work ONE issue by hand while the Harness fleet is paused or usage-HELD — check the precondition, show the issue's cost forecast against live usage and an APPROVE/DENY recommendation, let the human decide, then work the approved issue in this session with a budget re-check before each phase. Trigger on /harness-one or "work one issue while the fleet is paused". (user)

commands.name: harness-pause
commands.description: Pause the Harness fleet — drain (stop claiming new work) or checkpoint each agent to GitHub. Trigger on /harness-pause or "pause the agents". (user)

commands.name: harness-plan

commands.name: harness-prd

commands.name: harness-resume
commands.description: Resume a paused Harness fleet — clears the pause and continues here or via crash-recovery sweep. Trigger on /harness-resume or "resume the agents". (user)

commands.name: harness-start
commands.description: Launch the Harness worker pool for this project. Trigger on /harness-start or "start the fleet". (user)

commands.name: harness-status
commands.description: Show the Harness fleet dashboard — the workers and the issue each is running, what's complete vs stuck, complete vs stuck. Trigger on /harness-status or "what's the harness doing". (user)

commands.name: harness-stop
commands.description: Stop the Harness worker pool. Trigger on /harness-stop or "stop the fleet". (user)

commands.name: harness-uninstall
commands.description: Tear down a Harness install/project — remove the shared engine, this project's .harness/, and the /harness skills. Trigger on /harness-uninstall or "uninstall harness", "remove the harness install". (user)

commands.name: subagent-task-tree
commands.description: Execute a multi-task implementation plan as a chained subagent tree — you are the parent controller; you spawn one manager per task; each manager spawns a planner, a plan-auditor, one implementer per subtask, per-subtask auditors, and a final drift-auditor. Use when the user wants to "implement each task using subagents", asks for chained/nested subagents, a manager-per-task build, or subagent-driven execution of a plan/spec with audit gates at every level. (user)

commands.name: to-issues
commands.description: Break a plan, spec, or PRD into independently-grabbable issues on the project issue tracker using tracer-bullet vertical slices. Use when user wants to convert a plan into issues, create implementation tickets, or break down work into issues. (user)

commands.name: to-prd
commands.description: Turn the current conversation context into a PRD and publish it to the project issue tracker. Use when user wants to create a PRD from the current context. (user)

commands.name: writing-plans
commands.description: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code (user)

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

(claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: built-in-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

(user)

commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: built-in-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

(claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

## Problem Statement

A one-person online shop keeps its catalogue, stock movements and customer orders in three plain text files (`catalog.txt`, `movements.txt`, `orders.txt`). The owner has no tool to answer: what is on the shelves and what needs buying, what an order costs (volume/order discounts, per-line tax, exact to the penny), and what can ship today. Mistakes in the hand-edited files must be reported by file and line.

## Solution

A Python 3.9+ package **stockroom**, standard library only, installable with `pip install .`. It gives both an importable library (`import stockroom`) and a `stockroom` console command. It has two halves, built in order: the **shelves** (parse the catalogue and movements, stock levels, low stock, history, receive/ship) and the **orders** (parse orders, pricing, quote, fulfil, invoice, report). The orders half depends on the shelves.

The full behavioural spec is the **Original request** at the bottom. It is the top authority. This PRD only adds the decisions the request leaves open.

## User Stories

1. As the shop owner, I want `stockroom stock` to list every product with its on-hand count and an ok/low/out status, so I can see the shelves at a glance.
2. As the owner, I want `stockroom low` to tell me what to buy, and how many, to get back to twice the reorder level.
3. As the owner, I want `stockroom history SKU` to show every movement of a product with a running balance.
4. As the owner, I want `stockroom receive` / `ship` to append a validated movement, so the file never gets into a broken state.
5. As the owner, I want `stockroom quote ORDER` to price an order exactly (volume discount, order discount, per-line tax).
6. As the owner, I want `stockroom fulfil ORDER DATE` to ship what the shelves can cover without breaking later movements, and to tell me what is backordered.
7. As the owner, I want `stockroom invoice ORDER` to price only what has shipped.
8. As the owner, I want `stockroom report` in text, CSV or JSON to see all orders' status and money.
9. As the owner, I want every mistake in my files reported with the file name and line number, with exit status 1.
10. As a script writer, I want `parse_catalog`, `parse_movements`, `parse_orders`, `stock_levels` and `price_order` with typed results (`Decimal`, `date`, `int`), plus `ParseError` (a `ValueError` with `.line`).
11. As a script writer, I want `--json` output on the read commands, so I can pipe results into other tools.

## Implementation Decisions

**Layout / packaging**
- `pyproject.toml` (setuptools backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no dependencies), `[project.scripts] stockroom = "stockroom.cli:main"`. A package `stockroom/` with `__init__.py` re-exporting the public API, plus `__main__.py`, so `python -m stockroom` works the same as the command. Suggested modules: `parsing.py` (text → records, `ParseError`), `shelves.py` (stock levels, timeline, low, history), `pricing.py` (`price_order`), `orders.py` (shipped-so-far, fulfil planning, status), `cli.py`. Python 3.9-compatible syntax only (no `match`, no runtime `X | Y` unions).
- Records are frozen dataclasses: `Product(sku, name, price, reorder, tax)`, `Movement(date, sku, quantity, note, line)`, `Order(id, date, customer, lines, line)`, `Quote(lines, subtotal, order_discount, tax, total)`, `QuoteLine(sku, quantity, unit, gross, discount, net, ...)`. Extra fields such as the source line number, the share of the order discount, taxable amount and line tax are allowed.

**Text handling (all three files)**
- Decode as UTF-8 (strict). Strip one leading U+FEFF. Split lines on `"\n"` only, then drop one trailing `"\r"`. Never use `str.splitlines()`: it also splits on lone CR, VT, FF, U+2028 and others. A lone `\r` elsewhere stays part of the line.
- "Whitespace" for trimming and separating means ASCII space and tab only. A line is blank when it holds only spaces and tabs. It is a comment when its first non-space/tab character is `#`.
- All numeric and letter patterns are ASCII-only: use `[0-9]` / `[A-Za-z]` (or `re.ASCII`), never bare `\d` or `str.isdigit()`. Never pass unchecked text to `int()` or `Decimal()`, since those accept Unicode digits, `_`, whitespace, `NaN` and similar. Validate with a full-match regex first.
- Price: `[0-9]+(\.[0-9]{1,2})?`, value ≥ 0.01. Reorder: `[0-9]+`. Movement quantity: `[+-]?[0-9]+`, non-zero. Order line quantity: `[0-9]+`, ≥ 1. Date: `[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}` that `datetime.date` accepts. SKU: `[A-Za-z]{2,4}-[0-9]{3}`, normalised to upper case. Order id: `[Ss][Oo]-[0-9]+`, upper-cased. Uniqueness is checked on the upper-cased form (`so-7` duplicates `SO-7`; `SO-7` and `SO-007` differ).
- Catalogue line: split on `|`; there must be 4 or 5 fields, each trimmed; an empty 5th field is an error (the tax word must be valid when the field is present). Movement line: `DATE SKU QTY` plus the optional note; the note is the rest of the original line after the third field's separator, trimmed of spaces and tabs at both ends (inner whitespace kept as written). Order line: exactly 4 space/tab-separated fields. LINES split on `,`; each part must full-match `SKU*QTY`, so an empty part or a space is an error; a duplicate SKU in one order is an error.
- Error order: lines are validated in file order and the first bad line is raised. For movements, the stock-never-below-zero check runs after every line has parsed. It walks the movements sorted stably by date and raises on the file line number of the movement that first takes a SKU below zero.
- `ParseError(ValueError)` carries `.line` (int). Its message includes `line N: <reason>`. The CLI prints `stockroom: <file> line N: <reason>` to stderr. Reasons should be specific (e.g. `bad price '12.505'`, `unknown SKU 'ZZ-999'`, `duplicate SKU 'AB-100'`, `stock of AB-100 would go below zero (-2)`).

**Pricing**
- Use `Decimal` throughout. Every rounding is `quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)`. Rates: standard 0.20, reduced 0.05, zero 0. Volume discount: 10 % at qty ≥ 50, else 5 % at qty ≥ 10. Order discount: 3 % of the subtotal when the subtotal is ≥ 500.00. Allocation by largest remainder: each line's exact share is `D × net_i / subtotal`; floor it to the penny on its magnitude; hand the leftover pennies one each to the largest fractional remainders, the earlier line winning a tie. Taxable = net − share. Tax per line is rounded, then summed. Total = subtotal + order_discount (negative) + tax.
- Discounts are stored as zero or negative. Never produce `-0.00`; normalise a zero to `Decimal("0.00")`. Amounts print with exactly two decimals.

**Shelves semantics**
- "Order they count" = sorted stably by date, ties keep file order. `stock_levels` covers every catalogue SKU (0 when it never moved).
- Status: `out` when onhand == 0; `low` when 0 < onhand ≤ reorder; `ok` otherwise. A product with reorder 0 and onhand 0 is `out`. `low` lists the `low` and `out` products with `buy = max(1, 2*reorder - onhand)`. Everything is sorted by the upper-case SKU string.
- `receive`/`ship`: refusals (exit 1, the file byte-for-byte unchanged): an unknown SKU (malformed SKU text included); a quantity that is not `[0-9]+` ≥ 1 (so `-3`, `+3`, `0`, `abc` are all refused); a note containing `\n` or `\r`; a movement that would take stock below zero at any point in date order once appended. The note is trimmed of spaces/tabs; an empty note means no note. The movement is checked by appending it to the parsed list and re-running the timeline check. The write appends bytes in binary mode: `\n` first if the file is non-empty and does not end in `\n`, then `DATE SKU ±N[ NOTE]\n`, with the SKU upper-cased. Create the file when it is missing. Print the same line.
- `history SKU`: an unknown or malformed SKU is refused (exit 1).

**Orders semantics**
- Shipped-so-far for (order, sku) = min(ordered qty, Σ|qty| over movements with qty < 0, that SKU, and note exactly equal to `order <ID upper>`, case-sensitive), across all movements regardless of date. Owed = ordered − shipped.
- Fulfil on DATE: an unknown order is refused (1); a DATE before the order date is refused (1); a CLI date that is malformed or does not exist is exit 2. For each line, available = min(balance after every movement dated ≤ DATE, min balance after each movement dated > DATE). That is the largest N for which appending `-N` at the end of the file (which lands it last among DATE's movements) keeps every balance ≥ 0. Floor it at 0. Ship = min(owed, available). Append one movement per line with ship > 0, in order-line order, with the same newline rule as `receive`. If nothing is shipped, leave the file untouched. Then print `SKU shipped N backordered M` for every order line, then the status recomputed after the shipment. Exit 0 even if nothing shipped.
- Status (used by fulfil and report): `complete` if owed == 0 on every line; `open` if shipped == 0 on every line; `partial` otherwise.
- Invoice = `price_order` on a copy of the order whose lines carry the shipped quantities, with zero lines dropped. All the rules apply to those quantities (volume discount on the shipped quantity, order discount on the shipped subtotal). Nothing shipped is refused (exit 1). The header is `invoice ORDER DATE CUSTOMER`. In JSON, invoice uses the same object shape as quote.
- Report: sorted by (order date, numeric value of the order number, then the id string). Text: `ORDER DATE CUSTOMER STATUS SHIPPED/ORDERED QUOTED INVOICED`. CSV: the `csv` module, `lineterminator="\n"`, minimal quoting (a customer word may contain a comma or quote), the header `order,date,customer,status,ordered,shipped,quoted,invoiced`. JSON: the same keys in that order; ordered/shipped as ints; quoted/invoiced as two-decimal strings (`"0.00"` when nothing shipped).

**CLI**
- A hand-rolled argument parser (not argparse; argparse's abbreviation, `--` and negative-number handling get in the way of the "taken as typed" rule). Exit-2 checks run first: no command, an unknown command, `--dir` with no value, an unknown option, a bad `--format` value, the wrong number of positionals, a mistyped DATE (receive/ship/fulfil). Then the files are read: a missing `catalog.txt`, a missing or unreadable folder, a path that is a directory, an OS error or invalid UTF-8 are all exit 2 with a message on stderr. A missing movements/orders file counts as empty. Then the request runs, and refusals and data mistakes are exit 1.
- `--dir DIR` and `--dir=DIR` are accepted anywhere on the line, for every command; the last one wins. `--json` (stock/low/history/quote/invoice) and `--format X` / `--format=X` (report only) are accepted anywhere for those commands. Any other argument starting with `-` (`-` alone excluded) is an unknown option, exit 2. That covers abbreviations: `--js` is unknown. Exception: for `receive`/`ship`/`fulfil`, every argument other than `--dir`/`--dir=` is positional, as typed. So `ship D AB-100 -3` gives the quantity `-3` (refused, exit 1), and `receive D AB-100 3 --json` gives the note `--json`. `receive`/`ship` take 3 or 4 positionals; `fulfil` exactly 2; `history`, `quote` and `invoice` exactly 1; `stock`, `low` and `report` none. `-h`/`--help` prints usage to stdout and exits 0 (before anything else).
- Each command reads only its files: the shelves commands read the catalogue and movements; `quote` the catalogue and orders; `fulfil`, `invoice` and `report` all three.
- Output: the whole output is built in memory first, then written UTF-8-encoded to `sys.stdout.buffer` with `\n` line endings. On error nothing at all goes to stdout. JSON uses `json.dumps(..., indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` plus a trailing newline, with keys in the order listed in the request. BrokenPipeError on write or flush: point stdout at devnull and exit 0 quietly.
- `main(argv=None) -> int` is testable in-process. The console script wraps it with `sys.exit(main())`.

## Testing Decisions

- Use stdlib `unittest` only, under `tests/`, run with `python -m unittest discover -s tests`. No pytest dependency (a pytest run may still discover them).
- Test external behaviour only: the library API through `import stockroom`, and the CLI through `subprocess` running `[sys.executable, "-m", "stockroom", ...]` in a temp dir, plus in-process `main([...])`. Assert on stdout, stderr (file name + `line N`), exit codes, and the bytes of the file after writes (unchanged on refusal).
- The brief's examples must reproduce exactly (`stock` and `quote SO-1001` output).
- Pricing tests: hand-computed cases for the 5 %/10 % thresholds (9/10/49/50), the £500 boundary, allocation with remainder ties, `ROUND_HALF_UP` at 0.005, mixed tax rates, no `-0.00`.
- Parsing tests: each rule in the request, one bad-input case per rule, plus BOM, CRLF, lone CR, Unicode digits (`١٢`), `int()`-accepted junk (`1_0`), an empty 5th catalogue field, and below-zero detection in date order (the error line is the offending movement's file line, not the last line).
- Fulfil tests: a later movement capping availability, partial and backordered results, repeated fulfil reaching complete, a date before the order refused, a missing trailing newline in the file.
- A packaging smoke test: `pip install .` into a temp venv gives `stockroom` on PATH and `import stockroom` (it may be skipped when there is no network or venv).

## Out of Scope

- Third-party packages, a config file, locales or currencies other than GBP, editing or deleting existing lines, concurrency/locking between simultaneous runs, a GUI or web UI, and options beyond those listed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` installs the importable `stockroom` package and a `stockroom` console script; Python ≥ 3.9, stdlib only; `python -m stockroom` works the same.
- [ ] `parse_catalog` / `parse_movements` / `parse_orders` return the documented types and fields; any rule violation raises `stockroom.ParseError` (a `ValueError`, `.line` set, message contains `line N`) at the correct line, counting blank and comment lines.
- [ ] BOM ignored; LF and CRLF line ends only; blank lines and `#` comment lines ignored; ASCII-only digit/letter validation.
- [ ] Movements are validated in date order (stable on the same day); the line that first takes stock below zero is the reported mistake.
- [ ] `stock_levels` returns every catalogue SKU; `price_order` follows Prices steps 1–6 exactly (half-up, largest-remainder allocation with earlier-line tie-break, per-line tax), all two-decimal Decimals, discounts ≤ 0.
- [ ] `stock`, `low`, `history` output (text and `--json`) matches the request, including the brief's `stock` example byte for byte.
- [ ] `receive` / `ship` append exactly one correctly formatted line (adding a missing final newline first, creating the file if absent) and print it; every refusal leaves the file byte-identical and exits 1.
- [ ] `quote` output (text and `--json`) matches the request, including the brief's `quote SO-1001` example byte for byte.
- [ ] `fulfil` ships min(owed, available-on-DATE-without-breaking-later-movements) per line, appends `DATE SKU -N order SO-…` lines, and prints the per-line and status lines; a date before the order date is refused.
- [ ] `invoice` prices the shipped quantities with the same rules and layout (header prefixed `invoice `); nothing shipped is refused.
- [ ] `report` in text/csv/json with the documented columns, ordering, and types.
- [ ] Each command reads only the files it needs; a missing catalogue is exit 2; missing movements/orders files count as empty.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 on success; 1 for data mistakes and refusals (stderr names the file and line; stdout empty); 2 for unreadable files and command-line errors, checked in the order command line → files → request.
- [ ] `--dir` works anywhere; options must be spelled in full; `receive`/`ship`/`fulfil` take every non-`--dir` argument as typed.
- [ ] A closed stdout pipe (`stockroom stock | head -1`) exits 0 with no traceback.
- [ ] A `unittest` suite under `tests/` covers the above and passes with `python -m unittest discover -s tests`.

- Decode as UTF-8 (strict). Strip one leading U+FEFF. Split lines on `"\n"` only, then drop one trailing `"\r"`. Never use `str.splitlines()`: it also splits on lone CR, VT, FF, U+2028 and others. A lone `\r` elsewhere stays part of the line.
- "Whitespace" for trimming and separating means ASCII space and tab only. A line is blank when it holds only spaces and tabs. It is a comment when its first non-space/tab character is `#`.
- All numeric and letter patterns are ASCII-only: use `[0-9]` / `[A-Za-z]` (or `re.ASCII`), never bare `\d` or `str.isdigit()`. Never pass unchecked text to `int()` or `Decimal()`, since those accept Unicode digits, `_`, whitespace, `NaN` and similar. Validate with a full-match regex first.

Date: `[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}` that `datetime.date` accepts. SKU: `[A-Za-z]{2,4}-[0-9]{3}`, normalised to upper case. Order id: `[Ss][Oo]-[0-9]+`, upper-cased. Uniqueness is checked on the upper-cased form (`so-7` duplicates `SO-7`; `SO-7` and `SO-007` differ).
- Catalogue line: split on `|`; there must be 4 or 5 fields, each trimmed; an empty 5th field is an error (the tax word must be valid when the field is present). Movement line: `DATE SKU QTY` plus the optional note; the note is the rest of the original line after the third field's separator, trimmed of spaces and tabs at both ends (inner whitespace kept as written). Order line: exactly 4 space/tab-separated fields. LINES split on `,`; each part must full-match `SKU*QTY`, so an empty part or a space is an error; a duplicate SKU in one order is an error.
- Error order: lines are validated in file order and the first bad line is raised. For movements, the stock-never-below-zero check runs after every line has parsed. It walks the movements sorted stably by date and raises on the file line number of the movement that first takes a SKU below zero.
- `ParseError(ValueError)` carries `.line` (int). Its message includes `line N: <reason>`. The CLI prints `stockroom: <file> line N: <reason>` to stderr. Reasons should be specific (e.g. `bad price '12.505'`, `unknown SKU 'ZZ-999'`, `duplicate SKU 'AB-100'`, `stock of AB-100 would go below zero (-2)`).

**Pricing**
- Use `Decimal` throughout. Every rounding is `quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)`. Rates: standard 0.20, reduced 0.05, zero 0. Volume discount: 10 % at qty ≥ 50, else 5 % at qty ≥ 10. Order discount: 3 % of the subtotal when the subtotal is ≥ 500.00. Allocation by largest remainder: each line's exact share is `D × net_i / subtotal`; floor it to the penny on its magnitude; hand the leftover pennies one each to the largest fractional remainders, the earlier line winning a tie. Taxable = net − share. Tax per line is rounded, then summed. Total = subtotal + order_discount (negative) + tax.
- Discounts are stored as zero or negative. Never produce `-0.00`; normalise a zero to `Decimal("0.00")`. Amounts print with exactly two decimals.

**Shelves semantics**
- "Order they count" = sorted stably by date, ties keep file order. `stock_levels` covers every catalogue SKU (0 when it never moved).
- Status: `out` when onhand == 0; `low` when 0 < onhand ≤ reorder; `ok` otherwise. A product with reorder 0 and onhand 0 is `out`. `low` lists the `low` and `out` products with `buy = max(1, 2*reorder - onhand)`. Everything is sorted by the upper-case SKU string.
- `receive`/`ship`: refusals (exit 1, the file byte-for-byte unchanged): an unknown SKU (malformed SKU text included); a quantity that is not `[0-9]+` ≥ 1 (so `-3`, `+3`, `0`, `abc` are all refused); a note containing `\n` or `\r`; a movement that would take stock below zero at any point in date order once appended. The note is trimmed of spaces/tabs; an empty note means no note. The movement is checked by appending it to the parsed list and re-running the timeline check. The write appends bytes in binary mode: `\n` first if the file is non-empty and does not end in `\n`, then `DATE SKU ±N[ NOTE]\n`, with the SKU upper-cased. Create the file when it is missing. Print the same line.
- `history SKU`: an unknown or malformed SKU is refused (exit 1).

**Orders semantics**
- Shipped-so-far for (order, sku) = min(ordered qty, Σ|qty| over movements with qty < 0, that SKU, and note exactly equal to `order <ID upper>`, case-sensitive), across all movements regardless of date. Owed = ordered − shipped.
- Fulfil on DATE: an unknown order is refused (1); a DATE before the order date is refused (1); a CLI date that is malformed or does not exist is exit 2. For each line, available = min(balance after every movement dated ≤ DATE, min balance after each movement dated > DATE). That is the largest N for which appending `-N` at the end of the file (which lands it last among DATE's movements) keeps every balance ≥ 0. Floor it at 0. Ship = min(owed, available). Append one movement per line with ship > 0, in order-line order, with the same newline rule as `receive`. If nothing is shipped, leave the file untouched. Then print `SKU shipped N backordered M` for every order line, then the status recomputed after the shipment. Exit 0 even if nothing shipped.

- Invoice = `price_order` on a copy of the order whose lines carry the shipped quantities, with zero lines dropped. CSV: the `csv` module, `lineterminator="\n"`, minimal quoting (a customer word may contain a comma or quote), the header `order,date,customer,status,ordered,shipped,quoted,invoiced`.
